Messages.Author: Anthony Barker
Messages.Body:
The following situation happened the other day in tournament where we
had 4 Methuselahs, seated in the following order: Blood Brothers,
Obf/Dom, !Salubri, Gargoyles. The Blood Brothers Methuselah offered to
oust himself to the Gargoyle deck if he were able to obtain 1 VP for
himself. Given the state of game listed below, is this deal legal in
terms of maximising VPs/GWs, and what considerations should the judge
use in making their decision (e.g., game state)?

The state of the game is included below...

40 minutes left in the game.

Blood Brothers - 14 pool.
Mark - 4 blood, Blood Doll, Fortitude
Truman - 4 blood
Karl - 6 blood
3 uncontrolled vampires with 1 blood each.

Obf/Dom - 11 pool. 1 Victory Point.
Ohanna - 1 blood.
Laurent - 2 blood
Ingrid - 4 blood

Salubri Antitribu - 12 pool
Thomas - 4 blood
Adonai - 2 blood. Rack.
Wolf - 3 blood. Crimson Sentinel, Garotte, Auspex.

Gargoyles - 13 pool.
Erinyi - 3 blood.
Obsidian - 2 blood, Armor of Terra
Ferox - 4 blood, Armor of Terra, Masochism.
Powerbase: Chicago - 1 blood.

Cheers,

Anthony Barker.

Messages.Author: Ira

Hey All,

I completely and respectfully disagree with The Lasombra that
dealmaking including VPs is unsportsmanlike. What definition of
"sportsmanlike" are you using? The one that I use is:

- Try to get a GW.
- If there's no reasonable possibility of getting a GW, maximize VPs.
- If there's no reasonable possibility of getting any VPs, do whatever
you want.

"Reasonable" is defined by the judge at the time, but I personally
define it as at least a 5% - 10% chance.

> It's probably neither wise nor accurate to generalize women like this;
> I know some fine female gamers, as competitive as anyone.

I think you can go ahead and change that "probably" to a
"definitely."

Finally, regarding the specific example, I think a lot of depends on
the forward pressure of the gargoyles. If there were several force of
will + daring the dawn, then I could see the brood blothers being more
afraid and willing to deal (since they don't have bounce.) It does
seem like a potentially illegal deal to me, though.

Ira

Continuing the analogy, not if that one man is twice my size or
holding a weapon. You're assuming 1v1 is a "fair" fight. In VTES, I
find decks/players are rarely equally matched. Besides, if you want
to win, you should be looking to create an "unfair" fight that
preserves your own resources so you can carry the table later on.

> The one that says I won't destroy the game for someone else by
> becoming an additional predator and ousting them when I can oust my
> prey by myself and attempt to win on my own the same way the rest of
> the table is playing.

I somewhat agree with this. Ideally, we should not interfere with the
predator-prey balance. However, I note the conditional "when I can
oust my prey by myself". What about when you face your foil as a
prey/predator? No deck can cover all the eventualities in VTES. When
that situation comes up, I think the smart move is to deal with the
table to get the foil gone, not keep bashing my head into a wall in a
vain hope that I alone can conquer all.

> The definition of sportsmanship that says "Let the best man win".

Commendable, yes. A good way to win, no.

> The person with the best whining skills or the best manipulation via
> discussion skills is not (necessarily) the best player at the table.

VTES is a game of manipulation (says so right on the box). The best
player, IMHO, is the one with the best deck, best negotiation skills,
and a solid dollop of luck (it is a card game after all).

I completely agree with Ira. And disagree with The Lasombra. Being
sportsmanlike can't overshadow the rules and purpose of the sport.
(Fisticuffs not being a sport I currently engage in I'll defer to The
Lasombra on the rules involved there, but as I play VTES I've got some
opinions on that.)

In VTES I don't have a problem with just one man, if I did I'd be
playing M:tG. I have a problem with between 2 and 4 others. If to
*win* as defined by the rules means I have to bring in help from
another table (and the rules somehow let me) I'd do it. Why? Because
the purpose of this game is to win, and table manipulation is a large
part of that. If I can get someone to help me win for a favor, heck
yes I'll make that deal. If their position is bettered by it cool, it
means that they're more likely to follow through.

I know a few people who have a problem with this, they came up playing
M:tG and like the control provided by the dueling format, there is
only one person and they are always the enemy. VTES isn't so clear
cut, its political, it involves manipulation and use of resources
(including the ultimate victory conditions) to help you get the top
position at a table. Don't like it? Sorry, really I am, because the
game should be enjoyable even when you're losing. You should at least
be learning something (like how to deal at a table.)

> The one that says I won't destroy the game for someone else by
> becoming an additional predator and ousting them when I can oust my
> prey by myself and attempt to win on my own the same way the rest of
> the table is playing.

My purpose is to "destroy the game for someone else." It's not to
make them hate VTES, nor to make them quit, but I WANT MY PREY GONE.
If I guess right in the meta-game then I get to totally destroy
someone. I take away their ability to play, and oust them as quickly
as possiable. Of course I try to be nice about it, but the purpose of
the game is to gain VP's. By ousting as efficiently as possiable I
can do that. If I can trade Vote damage for rushes against my prey's
intercept vampire, I'll do that in a second, so what that two people
now have two enemies, I'm moving towards my victory condition. A side
consideration (one that I'm not allowed to think about!) is making
sure that I'm not losing players. So in pick-up games, and when
teaching someone I play easy decks, weaning people up to a tournement
level of play. But in a tournement if I'm not playing to win I'm
doing everyone there a disservice.

> The definition of sportsmanship that says "Let the best man win".
>
>
> The person with the best whining skills or the best manipulation via
> discussion skills is not (necessarily) the best player at the table.

If they win, then they are. (not over time, or even in the next game,
but if they win the table they were the best player at the table.)
They may not be the most liked, but they were the best.

As an asside: if a deck sits down and can't do anything to oust it's
prey, and the prey likes it that way (Say an assamite attack deck
preying on an IC obediance/PTO monster) then what is wrong with a
deal? The assamite improves its position (0 vps -> whatever it can
deal for) and the vote deck doesn't have to waste its offensive votes
on its Predator, and assures itself a victory. does this suck for the
rest of the table if they can't do anything about it? Yes. Is it the
deal makers fault? No, they brought decks that win the metagame and
made a deal to enhance their position at that table. A similiar thing
happens when two combat decks sit next to each other. There is no
reason for them both to hurt their chances of winning by not wanting
to annoy the table.

Cameron Domer
Prince of Madison

Hello All,

> The definition of sportsmanship that says if you have a problem with
> one man, you will fight that man by yourself, not bring 5 friends and
> all beat him.

I do agree with this traditional definition of sportsmanship. I
think it also includes being a gracious winner and a gracious loser.

I guess what I was trying to say is that the tournament rules should
not use the word "sportsmanship" because the game itself isn't
sportsmanlike. For instance, deal breaking is CERTAINLY not
sportsmanlike, but that's completely allowed and adds a lot to the
game.

I'm asking you what rules you would apply to dealmaking that would
make the game more fun overall. Personally, I think the rules as they
are now make the game pretty good, and prevent collusion to a good
degree. The Lasombra, if you could propose something different, I
would certainly like to consider it.

> I am sure both you and all judges have a function algorithm for
> determining the likelihood of varying outcomes. Perhaps you would care
> to share it with the rest of the world. With my terrestrial knowledge
> of mathematics I am usually forced to keep trying to win under the
> assumption that I can.

Surely you admit that in some situations you have an extremely low
chance of winning. In those situations, it's good to try to dealmake
to get even 1/2 a VP. Usually the threat in those cases is
transferring yourself out. If you fail to negotiate successfully,
then IMO it's fine to follow through with your threat and just oust
yourself right there.

> I would love to see a judge tell me my play (other than specific card
> related issues) is illegal.

I think this is referring to dealmaking and collusion, which are
illegal. For instance, let's say you sit down at a table with your
good friend as your prey. He knows you need to get 2VPs to get into
the finals, and he has no chance of making the finals. He brings up
no minions during the game, and ousts himself as quickly as possible.
That would be an example of illegal play that the Judge should
disallow.

Ira

In practise, you get a slippery slope. It starts when you're teaching
the game to new players and so have to advise them as they play the
game. This plus social banter develops into competitive whining and
informal coordination. Then you get extended negotiations and formal
deals. Finally, you get cross-game vendettas, trade-offs and
collusion.

certain amount of banter but not much whining, finger-pointing or
haggling. In serious tournaments, players should be announcing their
actions, playing their cards but otherwise staying silent.

chess and bridge are played but they are quite cerebral games. Poker
players tend to like a fair amount of banter (Amarillo Slim never
stops talking, I gather) but this stops well short of making deals.

offer deals like "give me one VP and I'll give you the table" even if

contemptable. The best players are the ones who win tables on their
own merits, not the ones who bootlick their way to second.

people have a different set of priorities due to the perceived

support. Either way, balls to the people who'd rather come in second

>Tournament Rules 2.3 "Players are expected to behave in a respectful
>and sportsmanlike manner at all times." and 5.2 "players must not use
>profanity, argue, act belligerently toward tournament officials or one

Wrestling implies none of these things. It is quite possible to
wrestle in a fair and sportmanslike manner - see
http://www.ncaa.org/library/rules/2003/wrestling_rules.pdf for
details. The reason that you can't wrestle in VTES is the same as the
reason that you can't play VTES cards in the middle of a wrestling
match - it's not in the rules and so it's not part of the game.

Serious verbal wrestling has rules too - see
http://www.constitution.org/rror/rror--00.htm for example. Notice how
this stuff goes on for pages and yet the VTES rulebook contains almost
nothing of this sort. The closest it gets is to impose a time limit
of 10 seconds on vote stalling. And that's really just a timing rule,
not an excuse for a debate.

Andrew

Garfield wrote:

one another, then the winner becomes a matter of pure negotiation. [...] On

solitaire on your hands... So this is the reason you are limited to attacking

Garfield's inclusion of the predator/prey relation was his specific mechanic
for selecting what he felt was the proper balance between the extremes of a
pure negotiation game and a multiplayer solitaire game. "This artificial
structure [the pred/prey relation] gives rise to a compromise between these
two extremes."

In fact, the only limit he placed on diplomacy was the predator/prey relation.
You may wish that he'd created more restrictions on negotiation but he clearly
did not.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 21 Jul 2003 07:17:05 GMT, Robert Goudie wrote:

>So what makes a bad multiplayer game? If players can interact too freely with
>one another, then the winner becomes a matter of pure negotiation. [...] On
>the other hand, if players can't interact enough you have multiplayer
>solitaire on your hands... So this is the reason you are limited to attacking
>the person to your left, your prey."

You're confusing "interaction" with "negotiation". In Garfield's
view, the former was good, the latter was bad. In VTES, players
interact through the play of their cards - combats, bleeds, votes -
these are all quite interactive. He constrained this interaction so
that you usually interact with your predator and prey. There's
nothing in these quotes to suggest that he wanted players to negotiate
about this interaction. He wanted this to be a game of deck design
and tactics, not a popularity contest or debate.

And the fact remains that, while there are plenty of rules for card
play, there are no rules for negotiation. Therefore negotiation is

not part of the game.

Andrew

No. They have worked within the confines of the mechanic.

For true "free for all" play this:

Bleeds can target any Methuselah (including those with text that
says otherwise, like Night Moves, which are intended to be extensions,
not restrictions).

Other (D) actions that specify "prey" or "predator" are likewise
able to target any other Methuselah (Corruption, etc.)

When someone is ousted, each remaining Methuselah gets 1 VP.
If you're the only Methuselah left, get an additional VP (all of which
basically says: you win if and only if you're the last Methuselah
in the game).
If someone withdraws, that Methuselah (and only that Methuselah) gets
a VP.

Then observe the distance from that scene to the one RCG established -
the game with deals and such, but with predator-prey mechanics.

Let me know if you find "free for all" more enjoyable.

A deal between two players that they will play cooperatively so that one

Depends on the judge's criteria. But, if the 2 VP player can talk well,
a lot could be spun.

The prime example I could think of is that the player tells the judge
(privately, of course), "I have no intention of keeping the deal." When
the game is just down to the player and his dealmate, the player can't
be blatant and say, "Bleed for 3? Uh, no block. Bleed for 3? Uh, no
block...", but it's easy enough to throw a game if you want to.

Less...cheating...examples would simply be claiming that they could
possibly take out their prey, but it would be no sure thing, and would
certainly leave them in a dire situation (eg, two combat decks sitting
next to eachother), or, alternatively, to survive they would have to
remove their predator, which would leave them totally unable to attack
their prey (eg, a combat deck with a S+B predator). The player doesn't
have to claim they won't get any VPs otherwise -- they just have to
claim that they won't get 3 or more.

It seems (to me) there's a precedent that says that though you have to
play to maximize your VPs, that's read as "maximize them under
reasonable circumstances". The fact that you can oust yourself (or
allow yourself to be ousted) (0% possibility for another VP) compared to
staying in the game (which may have an incredibly small, but still
non-0% possibility for another VP) seems to support this. So even if
there's a chance the player could get 3+ VPs, the player can argue that
it's too small to be reasonable.

Finally, if the player is deadset on getting a tablesplit deal but is
turned down by the judge, all he needs to do is take a few lumps and
then point out his situation has deteriorated.

--Colin McGuigan

Yes. I would be satisfied with all concrete zero-pool actions being
illegal. ie, you may not Pentex Subvert someone when at 2 pool. You
may not transfer your last pool to a vampire. You may not Clandestine
Contract someone when at 1 pool, saying "but it may be blocked!" You
may not bid 5 for the Hostile Takeover when you only have 5 pool.

You MAY call Ancilla Empowerment when at 1 pool and 3 minions, because
it is not a concrete thing -- voting it down after gaining pool for
Bribes is under your own control, for example. You MAY take a Vast
Wealth action when on 1 pool even though you have both .44s and Leather
Jackets in your deck. You MAY put yourself on zero blood in combat
facing a minion with 1 strength at close range with Tension in the Ranks
in play and you at 1 pool, hoping to draw into a Fortitude prevent card.
(don't have a way to prevent the damage with the disciplines on you?
not legal. yes, that call can be made at 100% accuracy.)

What's the difference? In the top four actions you are depending on
someone else's assistance to stop you from dying; a Sudden Reversal, or
blocking the Contract, or someone bidding more, etc. All external
factors, not at ALL under your control.

In the bottom three, you can save yourself later in the action through
either getting lucky on the VW draw, getting lucky on the Fortitude
draw, or through voting down your own Empowerment.

It's actually a pretty easy line to draw. And it's overdue, IMO.

<salem_ch...@yahoo.com> writes:
>half an hour to get ousted after they think they're already dead?
>interesting.

Sure. Happens a fair bit.

The player can't do anything. The player can't go anywhere. But the
player is being kept there as a buffer, to stop *his* predator bleeding
you. Or similar sorts of things. You want some blood-gain but they've
got Klaus van der Veken which would shut your hunting ground down, or
something similarly improbable. So you rush his predator, to stop him
ousting him. He doesn't stand a cat in hell's chance of going anywhere
- he's never EVER going to get through you - but having him there as a
buffer suits you.

And with a highly tense, highly subtle game, a couple of turns of that
can easily turn into a long, long time.

Except that people aren't currently playing by that rule, and it's

For example, after transferring 4 of your last 6 onto a minion and
tapping out bleeding: "Since I can't block all his actions no matter

>> What possible excuse do you have, IN GAME CONTEXT, to not attempt to

>what came of it.

I know. That's why I reformulated the original question above to
isolate the circumstances according to "not blocking because I have
other defenses", and "not blocking because i'm hoping someone else will
save me". =)

>VTES is a very political game. I played in the NAC last weekend and I

>think we knew that.

Yes. Some of that should probably be removed, since I think it is
starting to unnecessarily penalize deck construction. Toolbox v. Focus
has always been a classically balanced scenario, but I think right now
toolbox is the ONLY way to go, since that's the only way you'll ever
have anything to offer in the inevitable deals that start coming up.

Not that I mind in-game deals, don't get me wrong -- but it's the ones
where VP start getting carved up and handed out that bug me. Again, I
think this is wandering off the subject here. =)

>Should I be able to win games by convincing other players they have no

>put it that way, but bluffing and (in-game) intimidation is certainly
>important strategy. Otherwise bruise & bleed decks wouldn't need any

I wouldn't want to remove bluffing and/or intimidation from the game at
all. But I don't see how either of the above could ever lead to
self-ousting, either. "I'll kill your minion if you don't block this
bleed that will oust you."

Unless it's Christian.

Judging from how many times people self-oust and/or threaten to, I'm

>>

>
>Maybe. I've seen players who (probably prematurely) consider their
>situations to be hopeless do something like that. "Hosed" depends on the

Can't legislate against bad play. If they're sufficiently premature
about it, though, then the self-oust situation isn't actually in play at
all... it's hard to be "premature" when you're at 3 pool.

I think what you're thinking of is more the scenario where someone gets
their first minion Rotschrecked and diablerized, and assumes their game
is completely lost, without considering if that might have been the only
Rotschreck in the deck. They immediately begin making deals to throw
away their VP to disrupt the table.

>perspective of the "hose-ee." A newbie might lose his favorite minion to
>torpor and consider his game over. A top player will still see a path to
>victory and keep fighting.

see above. sufficiently premature panic is not going to trigger the
self-oust, because they usually have 14 pool =)

>> If they can rush cross-table, why not rush upstream and try to kill all
>> their predator's minions?
>
>Would be a good plan. Occasionally, there are reasons it couldn't happen
>(Secure Haven, predator has better combat, etc.). I'll tend not to rush
>my predator if I'm very sure I'll be ousted right away anyway. Why ruin
>his game? I also won't go down without a fight. Why ruin my
>grand-predator's game? But if I think there's any chance rushing backward
>will give me a couple more turns at least, then I'll do it.

i don't think we're in disagreement anywhere here: take actions that
give you a chance to survive at least a couple more turns, because you
may be able to pull something out of nothing.

In the qualifier, I played POT Rush. I sat down in the 2nd round behind
someone who was playing !Gangrel Anarchs with Flesh of Marble, Claws,
and bleeds for 1. On the face of it, this means that I am just dead in
the water. But as it turns out, I hung in there and kept pushing at
him, and was able to steal 1VP from that game where I really shouldn't
have had any... because he ran out of Claws and Flesh right about when I
put Fame and a Haven on Zachary.

They are, however, definite from the player's perspective. Barring
outside assistance, you will definitely oust yourself. If you allow the
loophole of "outside assistance", you make the rule unenforceable,
because someone could ALWAYS DI the card or play Eagle's Sight, etc.

>>Wealth action when on 1 pool even though you have both .44s and Leather
>>Jackets in your deck. You MAY put yourself on zero blood in combat
>>facing a minion with 1 strength at close range with Tension in the Ranks
>>in play and you at 1 pool, hoping to draw into a Fortitude prevent card.

>there is nothing definate about going to torpor.

Well, this is pretty situational, really, and I was just using Fortitude
prevent as an example. An ANI/PRE minion can play Terror Frenzy, for
example, hoping to draw into a Staredown to avoid being hit. I can't
think of a contrived enough situation off the top of my head where it
would be illegal, but I did want to point out that there are probably
some situations where you can say "You're suiciding. There is no card
in the game that can save you if you spend the blood for that card." I
wouldn't expect them to arise very frequently if at all.

>>What's the difference? In the top four actions you are depending on
>>someone else's assistance to stop you from dying; a Sudden Reversal, or
>>blocking the Contract, or someone bidding more, etc. All external
>>factors, not at ALL under your control.
>

>but the directness of the pool cost.

The directness of the pool cost is inherent in the cost of the card
itself, however. Again, if you allow the loophole above regarding "but
someone else might save me!" then you make the rule unenforceable.

>>In the bottom three, you can save yourself later in the action through
>>either getting lucky on the VW draw, getting lucky on the Fortitude
>>draw, or through voting down your own Empowerment.
>>
>>It's actually a pretty easy line to draw. And it's overdue, IMO.
>
>i don't think your line is quite so easy. i am rather inclined to

I'm willing to sit and listen to examples as long as necessary. =)

>think _some_ line is necessary, though. a lot of my players mistakenly
>beleive it's illegal in tourney rules to suicide, and a lot of new
>players really hate to see it happen (which might contribute to
>difficulties keeping the new players playing).

It can be summed up as: Nobody likes a quitter.

In very few games is a resignation accepted. Chess is one, and it is
seen as a mark of respect because of the zero-luck factor, something
almost no other game has.

>I think a rule could be:
>
>You can try and get yourself ousted if you can't reasonably get any
>more vps.

I would never specifically permit any action other than "trying to win
at all costs", however. It just encourages people to do the wrong
thing.

>You can't directly spend your last pool yourself, though.

Reworded above:

You may not make transfers to a minion, or play a card whose cost would
oust you.

This implicitly permits transferring X-1 pool to a minion, where X is
your pool, without directly encouraging it.

>Implications:
>You're allowed to decline to block stuff that will kill you.

Yes. I don't like the idea of forcing people to block things, and I
don't think it's necessary to do so yet (although if it comes to that, I
don't have a problem with phrasing the rule in such a way to force
people to attempt to block or otherwise defend if they have an untapped
minion.)

I don't like the idea of forcing people to admit the contents of their
hands in some fashion -- hand information should be secret to the player
alone, and if he chooses to not play a Wake, that's his business. Not
to mention that hand contents are practically unenforceable and are a
slippery slope to even step onto.

>You can take actions that if unblocked (even if the target cannot
>block or whatever) will kill you.

Only if the "killing" is not part of the cost of the action.

>You can call a vote that will kill you (and you may vote in favour).

I do not believe you should be allowed to vote in favor unless by doing
so you will be also gaining at least one VP. (I don't want to rule the
"I nuke the table with Ancilla Empowerment and guarantee myself the Game
Win since I already had 1 VP coming in" plan away, because it's often
highly effective.)

>It's not as harsh a line as it could be, but it's easier to see, and
>prevents the standard 'transfer out' problem (thus giving all other
>methuselahs one last ditch effort to maniplulate the table to their
>advantage).

Exactly my point. If someone is on the slow decline or the fast decline
it doesn't really matter; what matters is that their predator still has
to take the action to remove them from the game.

So if you're at 1 pool and a minion with Aching Beauty is bleeding you,

Eh, not that much. It's key to focus on concrete things when possible.

>>I don't like this one. Suppose you have a bleed reduction card that
>>would keep you in against a bleed of 3 but not against a 5 or 6. You
>>should have the threat of AI available.
>
> What threat? You're ousted. I gain six pool.

The threat of being AI'ed so that the predator doesn't bleed for
5 or 6 and you stay in the game.

A TC and an AI in hand vs. a predator with Ozmo and a Govern with
no other bleed modifiers leaves your predator in a bind - she can
oust you (at the cost of his minion), or she can coax out the TC
and try again next turn.

Your proposed rule would leave Ozmo would be free to bleed with
Govern with no retaliation. The rule has benefited the predator's
game by giving him the gift of a ready Ozmo after the oust that
she otherwise wouldn't have.

> You have no threat other than a spiteful attempt to spoil your
> predator's game for having beaten you.

She hasn't beaten you until you're ousted. If she has to sacrifice
Ozmo to "beat you", then she'll have to decide if that sacrifice
is worth it. No need to spare her the decision and gift her a
ready Ozmo with her VP.

If you have 1 pool, a ready untapped minion with +1 strength, and
your predator's Sylvester Simms with 1 blood comes to bleed you,
then blocking with your only minion would be just a spiteful
attempt to spoil your predator's game for having beaten you? You
would rather the Methuselah be forced to not block and just go
out with a whimper? What if you had a maneuver in your hand? And
then what if you knew Sylvester's controller also had a maneuver?
And so on...

> If I have seen you play Telepathic Counter, yes, I may well bleed you
> for 5 or 6 when you are only at 3 pool... at which point you have two
> options: Reduce it below 3, or be ousted. If you can't reduce it below
> 3, you lose. Spending that 3 on AI is nothing more than spite.

Or rather, bleeding for 5 or 6 when your prey "has beaten you" by preparing
for big bleeds is nothing more than taking your lumps for the VP.

No free lunch.

If your predator is playing with an open hand and shows a Conditioning
and bleeds with a vampire with dom while you're at 1 pool, you would
call playing the Telepathic Counter to reduce the bleed by two and
thereby forcing the Conditioning (at the cost of a blood) "nothing more
than spite" as well?

No, you should be able to play the TC and cost your predator a
Conditioning from her hand and a blood from her vampire to get the VP,
just like you should be able to play the AI and cost her a minion to
get the VP.

In message <3F2FD700...@white-wolf.com>,
LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> mumbled something about:

>Derek Ray wrote:
>>
>> What threat? You're ousted. I gain six pool.
>
>The threat of being AI'ed so that the predator doesn't bleed for
>5 or 6 and you stay in the game.

I see. I suppose I am more easily able to directly reduce the equation
down to its relevant parts. With the prevalence of Dramatic Upheaval,
Kindred Restructure, and Rush combat, I'm not sure I'd ever hold off in
that situation... assuming I even actually knew the AI was in my prey's
hand.

You are of course well aware of my own opinion on strategy: failure to
go for the oust when the cards are in your hand is generally a massive
misplay. There have been situations in the past, and there will be
again in the future, where the circumstances are such that the statement
above is wrong; but given that V:TES is a limited-information game, I
don't see that it's ever possible to know that it's "safe" to hold back
for a turn (without of course additional information such as that gained
from Revelations).

>A TC and an AI in hand vs. a predator with Ozmo and a Govern with
>no other bleed modifiers leaves your predator in a bind - she can
>oust you (at the cost of his minion), or she can coax out the TC
>and try again next turn.

Again, this assumes that you have extra information from Revelations,
and that the table is "safe" to hold off for that turn, and that the
situation is actually Ozmo with a DOM skill card and a Conditioning in
hand, so he can bleed for 5 and make your TC useless as defense.

In the above situation, Ozmo can ONLY oust if he plays Govern and the
prey plays AI. Other three circumstances:

a) Ozmo plays Govern, prey plays TC and is at 1 pool
b) Ozmo bleeds for 2, prey plays TC and is at 3 pool
c) Ozmo bleeds for 2, prey ignores it and is at 1 pool

In the revised situation, Ozmo still has no incentive to hold off. If
he bleeds for 5, he'll get the oust instantly as AI gets played.
Otherwise, you still have scenarios b) and c) above; no matter what
happens, Ozmo is going to have to play Conditioning at some point. If
my prey is looking to AI Ozmo, then he will happily play the TC on
Ozmo's cardless bleed, forcing Ozmo to -still- bleed for 5 with the
Conditioning or wait two turns for the oust -- totally an unsafe play.

>Your proposed rule would leave Ozmo would be free to bleed with
>Govern with no retaliation. The rule has benefited the predator's
>game by giving him the gift of a ready Ozmo after the oust that
>she otherwise wouldn't have.

Yes. I have no problem with this particular benefit, because the
circumstances under which it may arise are so rare as to be almost
-never- seen. I have only seen a self-ousting AI once, myself; have you
seen it more often than that?

I have FREQUENTLY seen a prey at 4 pool chunk the AI as defense when
someone tried to finish them off -- I consider this an excellent play.
But since everyone would be aware of the "can't play something you can't
pay for without dying" rule in advance, surely the prey would realize
that his AI becomes useless at 3 pool, and would either try to play it
in advance or just discard it as worthless for the future.

As it stands now, AI is a worthless card at 2 pool. I have no problem
with changing that threshold to 3 pool, because the circumstances are
still the same: it's a case of not having the proper cards in hand to
defend oneself against ousting, for one reason or another.

>> You have no threat other than a spiteful attempt to spoil your
>> predator's game for having beaten you.
>
>She hasn't beaten you until you're ousted. If she has to sacrifice
>Ozmo to "beat you", then she'll have to decide if that sacrifice
>is worth it. No need to spare her the decision and gift her a
>ready Ozmo with her VP.

Well, this type of situation doesn't really matter one way or the other,
frankly -- it's sufficiently rare. What's actually under discussion is
whether this particular side effect of having a rule stating "You may
not play cards you cannot pay the cost of if the cost would oust you" is
still an overall good thing or not.

I don't consider the self-ousting AI to be a sufficiently common
scenario to weigh into the primary decision. Yes, I do consider that
burning your last 3 pool to burn your predator's vampire when you cannot
save yourself to be spiteful, solely due to the magnitude of the effect.
Either way it does not improve your current game, so no logical in-game
reason can be applied to the action -- and since it doesn't improve your
current game, it doesn't matter if the option is now removed from the
game.

>If you have 1 pool, a ready untapped minion with +1 strength, and
>your predator's Sylvester Simms with 1 blood comes to bleed you,
>then blocking with your only minion would be just a spiteful
>attempt to spoil your predator's game for having beaten you? You
>would rather the Methuselah be forced to not block and just go
>out with a whimper? What if you had a maneuver in your hand? And
>then what if you knew Sylvester's controller also had a maneuver?

Reducing it to the simplest argument: Block, probably be ousted, don't
block, definitely be ousted. I wouldn't force either a block or a
no-block.

Even though I can conceivably KNOW that due to the 7 Master cards in my
hand, if Sylvester is trying to "trap" me by suiciding himself for
victory then I will lose because I must strike-hands and cannot avoid
doing so, this doesn't fall under the intentionally-narrow scope of the
rule proposed. Losing a minion to torpor is also less significant than
having one burned, and in the above example, my predator KNOWS that
Sylvester will have to go to torpor in order to oust me in that fashion.
All the information is on the table, in contrast with the AI example
above.

Perhaps Sylvester doesn't intend to go to torpor because he has a Pulse
and is simply attempting to tap me out -- perhaps Sylvester is going to
cycle a maneuver, knowing that I will not maneuver back even if I can,
and then another minion will bleed me. This is a different situation
than playing a Master card whose effect ousts me, however; it is again a
case of being unable to have the cards in hand to defend oneself.

If the best counterarguments to "you can't play a card whose cost would
oust you, and you can't transfer your last pool" are all super-contrived
corner-case scenarios like the above, by the way, then the argument
"for" is already logically made.

>> If I have seen you play Telepathic Counter, yes, I may well bleed you
>> for 5 or 6 when you are only at 3 pool... at which point you have two
>> options: Reduce it below 3, or be ousted. If you can't reduce it below
>> 3, you lose. Spending that 3 on AI is nothing more than spite.
>
>Or rather, bleeding for 5 or 6 when your prey "has beaten you" by preparing
>for big bleeds is nothing more than taking your lumps for the VP.

My prey hasn't beaten me; he just got ousted. It cost me X resources to
do so, and X happened to include a minion at that point.

>No free lunch.

Not a problem. Changing the threshold from 3 pool to 4 is somehow
providing a free lunch to big bleeders?

>If your predator is playing with an open hand and shows a Conditioning
>and bleeds with a vampire with dom while you're at 1 pool, you would
>call playing the Telepathic Counter to reduce the bleed by two and
>thereby forcing the Conditioning (at the cost of a blood) "nothing more
>than spite" as well?

Hardly. One blood to pay for Conditioning doesn't even remotely compare
to a totally burned vampire.

>No, you should be able to play the TC and cost your predator a
>Conditioning from her hand and a blood from her vampire to get the VP,
>just like you should be able to play the AI and cost her a minion to
>get the VP.

Playing the TC doesn't oust you.

Playing the AI does.

Again, this is all just a side-issue as to whether or not such a rule
would be beneficial. Removing the ability to self-oust with AI and burn
your predator's minion on the way out is just not significant in
comparison to the potential benefits achieved by removing self-ousts
from the game.

Yes, and that is the current state of affairs. Now that we're back to
debating things that matter... ;)

The original proposition was: you shouldn't be able to transfer out,
under the assumption that transferring out guarantees a 0% chance of
winning, and we'd like people to all be at least TRYING to win, even if
it's only hanging in there by a fingernail and hoping to get lucky.
This was the impetus for the introduction of the "Game Win" tournament
rule.

The immediate counterargument was that if the intent is to stop people
from self-ousting, there are numerous ways to self-oust with Master
cards, not the least of which being paying the cost when you have
exactly that amount of pool.

The obvious modification to the rule led directly to the wording above;
rewritten more carefully, it would be:

"You may not play a card whose cost would oust you, and you may not
spend your last pool for a transfer or effect if doing so would cause
you to be ousted."

This wording is:

- narrowly scoped (playing a card, making a transfer, or any situation
where you can spend pool as part of an effect)
- narrowly applied (only affects a small portion of gameplay; does not
attempt to legislate broad strategy decisions or force active play on
part of players)
- clearly worded (easy to make rulings on)
- addresses a specific issue (self-ousting)

(I find it interesting that I am using many of the same criteria the
Supreme Court uses to rule on the constitutionality of laws, by the way.
Leads one to believe that the Founding Fathers may just have had
somethin' goin' on between their ears after all.)

>BTW, what happens under your proposed rule when you play an action card
>that costs pool but, during the course of the action, you lose enough
>pool so that paying the cost of the action will oust you? Are you ousted?
>Does the action fizzle?

Per your previous ruling on paying the costs of actions:

The acting minion/Methuselah pays as much of the cost as he/she is able,
and then the action fizzles if there is cost remaining that is unpaid.

So both: You are ousted and the action fizzles if there is cost unpaid.
The action also fizzles if the acting minion leaves play (cf. previous
ruling on Blood Brother Ambush playing Burning Wrath), so if you are
ousted by events in the course of an action, it naturally ends even if
the action would otherwise be successful.

I'm not sure there are any cards in print which would let this happen,
by the way, but it's comparable to this potential scenario: Assume two
new cards have been printed: Vagrant's Rush, an action card to enter
combat at 3 stealth, costing 1 pool, and Fog of Confusion, a reaction
card which allows you to change the target of a (D) action directed at a
minion you control to another minion you control.

I am at 2 pool. I play Vagrant's Rush and target Aaron Duggan, which is
legal by the above rule. Talley plays Fog of Confusion and selects
Moncada as the new target of my action. The action is successful, and
before combat is entered I am ousted by Moncada's special; the action
fizzles and my predator gains 6 pool.

>If your predator is playing with an open hand and shows a Conditioning

>call playing the Telepathic Counter to reduce the bleed by two and
>thereby forcing the Conditioning (at the cost of a blood) "nothing more
>than spite" as well?

This isn't entirely comparable.

By playing AI - assuming you *do* play it, and there isn't a cross-table
SR or some similar effect that may or may not exist - you will be
ousted.

By playing Telepathic Counter, you will be ousted if the Conditioning is
played *AND* you don't draw - say - a My Enemy's Enemy in the redraw.

Additionally, a lower amount on the bleed in the end (lowered by 2,
perhaps) may encourage another Methuselah to play Major Boon.

Which reminds me, I'm not certain if this has been ruled on in the past
or not, but it relates to this issue and should be brought up.

I oust my prey with an action modified by Daring the Dawn.
I am at 1 pool.
Tension in the Ranks is in play.

Daring the Dawn's current card text:

"Daring the Dawn: Action Modifier, Fortitude
[for] Vampires cannot block this action. -{The acting}- vampire takes 2
aggravated damage (not preventable) after the action {resolves}." (snip)

As I understand event ordering, this should be the sequence of events:

Action is successful.
Action resolves:
- Prey loses pool (per criteria set down by action)
- Prey is ousted
- I gain 1 VP
- I gain 6 pool
After action resolves:
- Acting vampire goes to torpor
- I burn 1 pool for Tension in the Ranks

Correct?

Contrast with sequence of events assuming the action is combat with a
Famous vampire:

Action to enter combat is successful.
Combat ensues:
- pre-range and maneuvers happen
- I strike to send prey's Famous vampire to torpor
- Prey strikes to send my vampire to torpor
- Strikes resolve:
---- Prey and I go to torpor simultaneously
---- Prey burns 4 pool for Fame + Tension, I burn 1 pool for Tension
---- Prey and I are ousted simultaneously
---- I gain 1 VP
---- My predator gains 1 VP
---- My predator gains 6 pool

etc.

The difference here being that combat is part of the resolution of the
action, and since I am going to torpor during the action itself, I no
longer have the 'window' to gain 6 pool before I am ousted. Right?
